bib.title: RARE: Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning Enhancement for Large Language Models

legacy_report:
```text
SOURCE: "RARE: Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning Enhancement for Large Language Models", Hieu Tran, Zonghai Yao, Zhichao Yang, Junda Wang, Yifan Zhang, Shuo Han, Feiyun Ouyang, Hong Yu (UMass Amherst and UMass Lowell). Preprint, arXiv:2412.02830v4 [cs.CL], 2 Jun 2025. The extraction prints no venue. Code is promised at github.com/fatebreaker/RARE.

COVERAGE: 83,401 of 83,401 chars read (all 26 pages: body, tables, limitations, references skimmed, appendices A.1-A.7). Figures 6, 8 and 9 are images, so their data is not in the extraction. Only the text around them was read.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: RARE adds two retrieval actions to rStar's MCTS reasoning search and replaces its discriminator with a retrieval-based factuality scorer. A6 generates several search queries from the main question and answers with the retrieved text. A7 retrieves for each sub-question and re-answers it. RAFS splits a reasoning path into statements, generates queries, retrieves, and labels each statement Supported or Not Supported. The path's score is the share Supported, and the highest-scoring path wins.
  number: none (mechanism)
  setup: MCTS with 4 rollouts for the 3B and 8B models and 2 for the 70B. RAFS uses the same backbone as the generator. No fine-tuning.
  quote: "The overall factuality score for the reasoning path is calculated as the proportion of supported statements, indicating the trajectory's factual reliability." Also: "we set the number of rollouts to 4 for LLaMA 3.2 3B and LLaMA 3.1 8B models, and 2 for the LLaMA 3.1 70B model."
  where: Sec 3.2-3.3, A.1 (pp. 3-5, 14)

- claim: Component ablation on LLaMA 3.1 8B. Each part adds a little and the full system is best.
  number: rStar 70.0, +RAFS 71.4, +A6 72.4, +A7 71.2, +A6+A7 73.2, full RARE 74.8 (accuracy %)
  setup: 250 MedQA samples, LLaMA 3.1 8B. A single run is reported, with no variance. The 250-sample size means a gap of 1-2 points is within noise.
  quote: "Configuration Accuracy rStar 70.0 rStar + RAFS 71.4 rStar + A6 72.4 rStar + A7 71.2 rStar + A6 + A7 73.2 RARE (rStar + A6 + A7 + RAFS) 74.8"
  where: Table 3, Sec 4.3 (p. 6)

- claim: On medical QA, RARE beats plain CoT, single-shot RAG (MedRAG), iterative RAG (i-MedRAG), self-consistency and rStar at every model size. On LLaMA 3.1 70B it beats GPT-4o on two of three benchmarks.
  number: Averages for 8B: CoT 62.76, MedRAG 64.81, i-MedRAG 71.21, SC 64.60, rStar 70.56, RARE 73.84. For 70B: RARE 84.51 vs GPT-4o 83.57. On MedQA, 87.43 vs 85.55. On MMLU-Medical, 90.91 vs 90.45.
  setup: MedQA, MedMCQA, MMLU-Medical. LLaMA 3.2 3B, 3.1 8B and 3.1 70B Instruct. The retrieval corpus is MedCorp with ColBERT. The paper says gains over rStar are p<0.01 by paired t-tests "over multiple runs", but gives no run count.
  quote: "RARE-enhanced LLaMA3.1 70B outperforming GPT-4o on MedQA (87.43% vs. 85.55%) and MMLU-Medical (90.91% vs. 90.45%)"
  where: Table 1, Sec 4.1 (p. 5). On MedMCQA, GPT-4o 74.70 vs RARE 75.18, which RARE also wins in the table.

- claim: Single-shot retrieval gives a small gain over CoT. Iterative retrieval gives much more.
  number: 8B averages: CoT 62.76, MedRAG 64.81, i-MedRAG 71.21. 3B averages: CoT 53.37, MedRAG 56.48, i-MedRAG 60.41. 3B MedRAG on MedQA is 52.08 vs CoT 52.63, so retrieval alone slightly hurt there.
  setup: Same as Table 1.
  quote: "MedRAG 63.00 56.87 74.56 64.81 ... i-MedRAG 73.61 61.61 78.42 71.21" (8B)
  where: Table 1 (p. 5). The comparison is my reading of the table, not a claim the authors state.

- claim: On commonsense QA, RARE beats rStar and in places GPT-4o. Gains are largest on multi-hop StrategyQA.
  number: 8B over rStar: +6.45 StrategyQA, +4.26 CommonsenseQA, +2.87 PIQA. 70B: 85.74 SQA, 86.98 CQA, 92.66 PIQA. Over CoT: +10.19 on StrategyQA, +7.22 on CommonsenseQA.
  setup: StrategyQA, CommonsenseQA, PIQA. LLaMA 3.1 8B and 70B. The 70B average is 88.46 vs GPT-4o CoT 86.09. GPT-4o still leads on CommonsenseQA (86.50) and loses to RARE there only narrowly (86.98).
  quote: "RARE's largest improvement over CoT is observed on StrategyQA(10.19%), where multi-step reasoning is crucial"
  where: Table 2, Sec 4.2 (p. 5-6). The text says RARE surpasses GPT-4o on all three at 70B. The table does not clearly show that for PIQA: 92.66 vs 91.13 is fine, and SQA 85.74 vs 80.64 is fine.

- claim: The factuality scorer agrees with medical experts about as well as the experts agree with each other.
  number: Inter-annotator agreement 86.49%. RAFS alignment 87.84% (annotator 1), 82.43% (annotator 2), average 85.14%.
  setup: 10 MedQA questions, answers from RARE with LLaMA 3 8B, about 100 statements. Two USMLE-passed annotators. The sample is tiny.
  quote: "Average RAFS-Annotator Alignment 85.14"
  where: Table 4, Sec 4.5 (p. 6)

- claim: The cost is large. RARE uses roughly 300 times the tokens of CoT and about 30% more than rStar.
  number: CoT about 400 tokens per example, rStar 92.6k, RARE 119.9k. Accuracy gain over CoT: rStar +4.52%, RARE +9.05%. This is averaged over the commonsense tasks.
  setup: Figure 6, averaged over commonsense tasks. No latency or dollar figures.
  quote: "CoT requires approximately 400 tokens per example, while rStar averages 92.6k tokens, and RARE increases this to 119.9k tokens due to its additional retrieval-augmented steps."
  where: Sec 4.6 (p. 6)

- claim: Retrieval gives smaller gains on tasks that lean on general commonsense than on multi-step ones.
  number: CQA +7.22 vs SQA +10.19 over CoT
  setup: Commonsense tasks, as above. This is the authors' interpretation.
  quote: "tasks relying more on commonsense knowledge rather than explicit step-by-step reasoning do not benefit as significantly from retrieval-augmented reasoning"
  where: Sec 4.2 (p. 5-6)

- claim: RARE can skip retrieval. Common winning paths include A1->A2 and A3->A2, which use no retrieval, alongside A1->A6 and A3->A7->A3. The authors present this as adapting between retrieval and no retrieval.
  number: none (the path charts in Figs 8 and 9 are images)
  setup: MedQA and StrategyQA top-10 paths
  quote: "RARE can also answer simple problems directly via step-by-step (CoT-like) reasoning without invoking retrieval."
  where: Sec 4.4, 5.2 (pp. 6-7)

- claim: A worked example shows how RAFS ranks candidate answers.
  number: Scores 1.0 (correct, ketotifen), 0.625 (wrong), 0.6 (wrong, warm compresses). Fig 5 shows 3 Supported and 2 Not Supported giving 0.6.
  setup: One MedQA-style case. The wrong paths score only slightly below 1.0, so the margin is thin.
  quote: "Candidate Reasoning 2 ... resulting in a lower factuality score of 0.625. Candidate Reasoning 3 incorrectly recommends warm compresses ... receiving a score of 0.6."
  where: A.6, Fig 7 (p. 14)

- claim: Retrieval setup used.
  number: MedCorp has 30.4M docs and 54.2M snippets. PubMed 23.9M, StatPearls 9.3k docs and 301.2k snippets, Textbooks 18 books and 125.8k snippets, Wikipedia 6.5M docs and 29.9M snippets. Textbook passages are capped at 1,000 characters.
  setup: ColBERT late-interaction retriever (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020). The paper reports no retrieval top-k and no retriever ablation.
  quote: "ColBERT's late interaction mechanism enables fine-grained token-level relevance matching"
  where: A.4, Table 5 (p. 13)

LIMITS
- The authors concede three points. Only open LLaMA models were tested, because proprietary models would need too many API calls. The method finds one correct path but does not optimise for the shortest or most robust one, and they name reward hacking as a risk. It uses MCTS with no trained reward model. The ethics section adds that it is English and text only, and not for clinical use.
- The paper does not show:
  - Latency, dollar cost or per-query retrieval counts.
  - A retriever or corpus ablation.
  - Any comparison with HyDE, query rewriting alone, or rerankers.
  - Confidence intervals or the number of runs behind p<0.01.
  - Any test on non-exam, real-world queries. All tasks are multiple choice or yes/no, and only 3 medical and 3 commonsense sets are used.
- The scorer is the same model as the generator (a self-scorer), and no check is shown against its own errors. Human validation covers about 100 statements from 10 questions.
- All iterative-RAG baselines (MedRAG, i-MedRAG) are medical-specific, and the paper does not state how they were configured for the commonsense tasks.
- Dated: the GPT-4o and Claude-3.5 baselines are 2024-era models.

BUILDS ON
- rStar (Qi et al., 2024): MCTS with five reasoning actions and a discriminator. This is the direct base, and RARE replaces the discriminator.
- MCTS (Browne et al., 2012) and UCT.
- Chain of Thought (Wei et al., 2022) and self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022).
- SAFE (Wei et al., 2024, "Long-form factuality in large language models"): RAFS adapts it, swapping GPT-3.5 for LLaMA and Google Search for corpus retrieval.
- i-MedRAG (Xiong et al., 2024b): multi-turn follow-up queries, which inspired A6 and A7.
- MedRAG and MedCorp (Xiong et al., 2024a).
- ColBERT (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020).
- SeRTS (Hu et al., 2024): MCTS-guided query generation. It is depth-first and one query at a time, while RARE's A6 issues several queries at once.
- Also cited: Self-BioRAG (Jeong et al., 2024), LLaMA 3 (Dubey et al., 2024), Trivedi et al. 2023 (IRCoT), Zhou et al. 2022 (least-to-most).

CODE: none. The appendix gives prompts only (A.7). The A6 prompt reads: "Given a question, generate a search query that would help gather information to answer it... The query should aim to obtain new information and be specific enough to ensure that the search results are relevant and helpful." The A7 template is "### Instruction: {user question} ### Relevant Documents: {relevant documents} ### Response:". The UCT formula is UCT_j = X̄_j + C·sqrt(2 ln N / N_j) (A.5, Eq. 1).

FIGURES (not extracted as data)
- Fig 1, p. 2: the pipeline of generator, factuality scorer and selection of the best path.
- Fig 5, p. 4: the four RAFS steps, with a worked 0.6 score.
- Fig 3 and Fig 4, p. 3-4: A6 compared with A7. A6 reuses entities from the question, and A7 uses entities from earlier sub-answers.
- Fig 6, p. 6: accuracy against generated tokens, which shows the cost trade-off.
- Figs 8 and 9, p. 15: the top-10 winning action paths.

PROBLEMS
- The extraction is clean text with no embedded instructions. Table 1 and Table 2 were flattened into rows, but the numbers read cleanly.
- The venue is not printed. Only the arXiv v4 stamp is given.
- Table 1 uses "MMLU-M" in its header and "MMLU-Medical" in the text.
- I did not run the figure-caption script. Fig 6, 8 and 9 data are image-only.
- Fit for the note: this is reasoning-time iterative retrieval with factuality scoring on exam QA, not a retrieval-quality ablation of the MRR and P@1 kind the note walks through. Use it only as support for "multi-query or iterative retrieval beats single-shot retrieval" and "verifying against retrieved evidence helps". The cost figures (roughly 300 times CoT's tokens) belong beside the note's latency discussion.
```
